title: Korean Nightlife 101: A Beginner's Guide to Hongdae, Itaewon, and Gangnam (Plus Drinking Etiquette)
html:
If you've only seen Korean nightlife in K-dramas or K-pop music videos, the real thing can feel confusing at first — where do you even start? This guide breaks down Seoul's three main nightlife neighborhoods (Hongdae, Itaewon, and Gangnam), explains Korean drinking etiquette so you don't accidentally offend anyone, and covers noraebang (karaoke rooms), the classic way a night out in Korea usually ends. Everything here is written for someone who has never been clubbing or drinking in Korea before.

Hongdae: The Young, Loud, and Budget-Friendly Side of Seoul Nightlife

Hongdae (short for "Hongik University area," in Mapo District) is the neighborhood around Hongik University, and it's the heart of Seoul's student and indie culture. The streets here are packed with small bars, dance clubs, live-music venues, and street performers — on weekend nights, you'll see free "busking" shows (singers and dancers performing on the street for tips) right next to the main entrance plaza known as Hongdae Playground.

Clubs here play hip-hop, K-pop remixes, and pop-EDM, and entry fees are the cheapest of the three areas — usually around ₩15,000–25,000 (about $11–18 USD), and many clubs include a free drink with that cover charge. The crowd is mostly Korean university students and twenty-somethings, so it's a good pick if you want an energetic, affordable first night out. Some bars and clubs stay open very late or even 24 hours on weekends.

Itaewon: Seoul's Most International Nightlife District

Itaewon, in Yongsan District, has historically been Seoul's most international neighborhood, originally because of the nearby U.S. military base. Today it's known for a genuinely mixed crowd of Koreans, expats, and tourists, restaurants from dozens of different countries, and a nightlife scene that leans toward techno and house music in small clubs with serious sound systems. The area is also full of daytime character — for example, Itaewon Antiques Street, a row of antique furniture and decor shops that's been there since the late 1960s, shows a completely different side of the neighborhood before the clubs open at night.


Itaewon Antiques Street — a daytime landmark in the same neighborhood that turns into one of Seoul's busiest nightlife areas after dark. (Photo: Korea Tourism Organization, via TourAPI)

One honest safety note: in October 2022, a crowd crush during Halloween celebrations in Itaewon's narrow alleys killed 159 people. Seoul now runs special crowd-safety measures (extra police, barriers, one-way pedestrian flow) during Halloween and other big nights. It's not a reason to avoid Itaewon — but on very crowded nights, stick to main streets, don't push through tight alleys, and leave early if an area feels packed beyond comfort.

Gangnam: Upscale Clubs, Bottle Service, and K-Star Road

Gangnam (yes, the one from the song) is Seoul's most polished and expensive nightlife district. Clubs here — Club Octagon is the most famous, regularly ranked among Asia's top EDM clubs — are bigger, dressier, and pricier than Hongdae's. Expect cover charges around ₩20,000–30,000, with VIP tables starting around ₩300,000 and up. Dress codes are stricter too: smart-casual at minimum, no flip-flops or athletic wear at most doors. Nearby K-Star Road, lined with K-pop idol statues, and the boutique-filled streets of Apgujeong make this a good area to dress up and bar-hop before a club.


The Gangnam and Seocho districts of Seoul. (Photo via Wikimedia Commons, public domain / CC0)

Korean Drinking Etiquette: What Locals Actually Do

You don't have to follow every rule perfectly as a visitor, but knowing the basics will help you fit in and avoid awkward moments. Soju is Korea's signature clear, bottled spirit (around 16–20% alcohol, sold almost everywhere), and it comes with its own etiquette:

  • Don't pour your own drink. At a table, people pour for each other, not themselves. If your glass is empty, someone will usually refill it — and you should offer to pour for others too.
  • Use two hands for someone older or more senior. When pouring for — or receiving a drink from — someone clearly older, support the bottle or glass with both hands as a sign of respect. Among close friends your own age, one hand is fine.
  • "Geonbae!" (건배) is the Korean toast, roughly "cheers" — clink glasses with everyone at the table, not just the person next to you.
  • It's okay to say no. If you don't want to drink or want to slow down, say so early and clearly. Koreans generally respect that, especially with foreign guests.

How locals actually do it: many nights out follow a pattern locals call 1차, 2차, 3차 ("first round, second round, third round") — dinner first, then a bar, then often karaoke. Nobody is obligated to stay for every round, so leaving after 1차 or 2차 is completely normal.

Noraebang: The Classic Way a Night Out Ends

Noraebang (노래방, literally "song room") is Korea's version of karaoke, but instead of singing in front of strangers, you rent a private room with your own group. Most rooms are booked by the hour, start around ₩20,000–30,000 per hour for a basic room (prices roughly double during peak weekend night hours), and come with a remote control, tambourines, and a song list that usually includes an English-language section alongside Korean, Japanese, and Chinese songs.

If you'd rather sing alone or skip the group commitment, look for a coin noraebang — a small pay-per-song booth, often just a few hundred won per song, that's common near subway stations and perfect for shy singers. Note that not every noraebang allows you to bring in or order alcohol, so ask staff first if that matters to you.

Before you go out — a quick checklist:

  • Bring your physical passport. Clubs in all three areas check ID, and a photo of your passport usually isn't accepted — bring the real thing. The legal drinking age for foreign visitors is 19 (international age).
  • Know your way home. Seoul's subway generally stops running around midnight to 1 a.m. depending on the line — check Naver Map or KakaoMap for your last train. After that, "owl buses" (marked with an N before the route number) run through the night, or you can take a taxi — night taxis add a surcharge of roughly 20–40% after midnight.
  • Stick with your group and keep your phone charged, especially in crowded areas late at night.

Quick comparison if you're deciding where to start your night:

AreaVibe / MusicTypical CoverBest For
HongdaeHip-hop, K-pop remix, indie/live bands₩15,000–25,000Budget travelers, young crowd, live music
ItaewonTechno, house, international bars₩10,000–20,000 (varies)Mixed international crowd, serious music fans
GangnamMainstream EDM/K-pop, bottle service₩20,000–30,000+Dressed-up splurge night, celebrity-spotting energy
